newsitem.title: UK: British unions oppose government on EU work hours.
newsitem.headline: British unions oppose government on EU work hours.

text.p: Britain's trade unions on Tuesday backed a European Court of Justice ruling that Britain should apply a European Union directive on working hours and said they would fight their government if it did not comply.

"I think this is very good news for British workers... This is a major contribution by the European Union," John Monks, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), told the British Broadcasting Corporation.
A spokesman for the umbrella union confederation said three affiliated unions were preparing test cases if the government refused to comply with the directive.

The biggest union, UNISON, which organises workers in public services, is expected to lead the way. Two other unions, which represent professional and managerial staff, are also planning court action if necessary.

The government is furious that the directive -- which limits the working week to 48 hours and gives workers a right to three weeks paid holidays -- was passed as a EU health and safety regulation, requiring only majority approval to become law.
Britain argues that it is an employment issue, which required a unanimous vote. It abstained when the rules were passed.
In a statement issued by the TUC, Monks accused Prime Minister John Major of holding the EU to ransom over the issue.
"Mr Major is blackmailing the rest of Europe because his government cannot accept defeat graciously," Monks said.
Major said on Tuesday he would continue the fight against the law, saying: "I believe it is a bad piece of legislation. I don't accept that it is appropriate to the United Kingdom."
The government and some employers say the directive will harm industrial competitiveness, but Monks said the rules were flexible and would, in fact, boost productivity.
"As good employers already know, a workforce that is treated well is more productive than an exploited and exhausted one," he said.
Britain is the only EU country where workers have no legal right to paid leave. According to TUC data, 2.5 million British workers -- 12 percent of the workforce -- have no paid holidays.
The TUC also said 30 percent of full-time employees in Britain work 46 hours per week or more, compared with nine percent in France and six percent in Germany.
